blocks.text: Some things in a system just sit there, the same set, every single time you ask about them.
A project has a README, a LICENSE file, and a handful of config files, and that list of names does not shift from one minute to the next just because you looked at it twice.
Static resources are MCP's way of modeling exactly that kind of stability, a known, fixed collection that a server can declare once and a client can rely on without constantly double checking.
This lesson is about what makes a resource static, why that property is valuable, and how a server actually declares a set like this.
1. What Makes a Resource Static

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A fixed resource list is defined once and stays the same

blocks.text: A resource is static when the set of resources a server offers, the actual list of URIs and names, is fixed and known at any given moment, not something that gets discovered, generated, or changed based on what a client asks for. If you call resources/list twice in a row on a server exposing static resources, without anything in the underlying system changing, you get back the exact same list both times, same URIs, same names, same order even.

This is a property of the list itself, not of the content behind each entry. A static resource can absolutely have content that changes, a config file can be edited, but the fact that config.yaml exists as an entry in the list is not in question from one call to the next. Staticness describes the shape of the collection, not whether anything inside it is frozen in time.

It helps to picture staticness on a spectrum rather than a strict binary. A truly static server never adds or removes entries without a redeploy, while a server further along the spectrum might refresh its list occasionally on a schedule, and a fully dynamic server recomputes its list on every single call. Most real servers sit closer to one end or the other, and knowing which end helps you design the right client behavior around them.
2. Real-World Examples of Static Resources

The clearest examples come from things that are enumerable by nature. A server exposing a project's source tree might list every file under a src directory, a fixed, known set determined by whatever is on disk when the server starts. A server wrapping an application's configuration might expose exactly the config files that ship with that application, no more, no less.

items: The set of config files shipped with an application, such as database.yaml, cache.yaml, and logging.yaml.
A fixed collection of documentation pages that make up a product's help center.
The handful of dashboards a monitoring tool ships with out of the box.
A style guide made up of a known, unchanging set of chapters.

blocks.text: Each of these has a defining trait: you could, in principle, write down the full list by hand ahead of time and it would stay accurate, because nothing about the domain calls for items being added or removed on the fly.

blocks.text: 3. Declaring a Static Resource List

On the server side, declaring a static resource list is often the simplest possible implementation of resources/list, a handler that returns the same hardcoded or startup-computed array every time it is called, with no branching logic based on server state that changes over the session. Many SDKs let a server author register a resource once, at setup time, and the framework takes care of surfacing it correctly whenever a client asks.

code.content:
# A minimal static resource declaration, pseudocode
RESOURCES = [
    {"uri": "config://app/database.yaml", "name": "database.yaml", "mimeType": "text/yaml"},
    {"uri": "config://app/cache.yaml", "name": "cache.yaml", "mimeType": "text/yaml"},
    {"uri": "config://app/logging.yaml", "name": "logging.yaml", "mimeType": "text/yaml"},
]

def list_resources():
    return RESOURCES

blocks.text: Some SDKs go further and let a server author declare each static resource with a decorator or registration call right next to the code that reads it, keeping the declaration and the read handler close together in the source file rather than maintaining two separate lists that can drift apart.
4. The resources/list Response Shape

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A resources list request gets back an array of resource entries

blocks.text: Whatever the server's internal implementation, the wire shape a client sees is the same JSON-RPC response, an array under a resources key, each entry carrying at minimum a uri and typically a human-readable name and a mimeType hinting at how to interpret the content once fetched.

A client seeing this response for a static server can reasonably treat it as the whole picture for the current session, there is no hidden fourth config file waiting to appear later unless the underlying files on disk genuinely change.

Some servers also include an optional annotations field on each entry, hinting to a client how a resource is best used, for instance marking one entry as intended primarily for a human reader versus another intended primarily to be consumed by a model.
5. Static Does Not Mean Content Never Changes

It is easy to conflate a static list with static content, but these are different guarantees. A server might expose database.yaml as a static entry, always present, always at that URI, while the actual bytes returned by resources/read for that URI change every time someone edits the file on disk. The list is stable, the content behind each item is not necessarily frozen at all.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Static describes the membership of the set, which items exist, not the freshness of what is inside each one. Resource versioning, covered later in this module, is what handles content changing over time.

blocks.text: 6. Static vs Dynamic: The Key Distinction

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A static list is compared against a dynamic one that is computed live

blocks.text: The opposite of a static resource set is a dynamic one, covered in depth in the next lesson, where the very membership of the list depends on something that shifts, a search query, live database rows, currently open browser tabs. The practical test is simple: if you can enumerate every entry ahead of time without running anything against live, changing state, the set is static.

blocks.text: 7. Why Clients Like Static Resources

Static resources are the easiest case for a client to reason about. A client can fetch the list once, present it in a menu or picker, and trust that menu without re-querying the server every few seconds. There is no risk of an entry silently vanishing between when a user sees it in a list and when they click it, which matters a lot for building a smooth, predictable user interface on top of an MCP connection.

This predictability also simplifies error handling. If a client tries to read a URI it previously saw in a static list and gets an error, that is a genuine anomaly worth surfacing, rather than an expected race condition against a constantly shifting backend.

This predictability compounds nicely with tool use in a broader agent workflow. A model that has already seen a static resource list early in a conversation can reference specific URIs by name several turns later without re-listing, confident the referenced entry still exists exactly as it did before.
8. Caching Static Resource Lists

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A client caches a static list after fetching it once

blocks.text: Because the list is not expected to change within a session, a client is free to cache the result of resources/list and avoid repeating that call unnecessarily. Some clients still re-fetch on reconnect or on an explicit user-triggered refresh, just to be safe, but there is no need to poll a static server's list every few seconds the way you might for something dynamic.

code.content:
# Client-side caching, pseudocode
if not cache.has("resources"):
    cache["resources"] = await session.list_resources()
resources = cache["resources"]

blocks.text: 9. Naming and Organizing Static Resources

Since the whole set is known up front, a server author has the luxury of designing clean, consistent names and URIs for every entry, rather than generating them programmatically on the fly. This is a good moment to think about hierarchy, grouping related config files under a shared authority or path prefix, so a client rendering the list can present it in a sensible, organized way rather than a flat, arbitrary pile.

items: Group related static resources under a shared path prefix, config://app/database.yaml and config://app/cache.yaml.
Give every entry a short, descriptive name field distinct from its full URI.
Keep ordering deterministic, alphabetical by name is a safe default, so the list looks the same across restarts.

blocks.text: It also helps to think about what a client, or a model acting on a user's behalf, will do with the list before ever reading a single resource. A well organized static list, grouped and named clearly, often lets a model pick the right resource on the first try, purely from the list metadata, without needing to read several candidates just to figure out which one is relevant.
10. Metadata: name, description, and mimeType

A static resource entry is a great place to invest in good metadata, since you are writing it once and it will be seen by every client that ever connects. A clear description field, in particular, helps a client, or a model acting through a client, decide whether a given resource is relevant without needing to fetch its full content first.
11. When a Static List Grows Too Large

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A small static list is compared against a list too large to send at once

blocks.text: A collection can start static and stay perfectly fixed while still growing large enough that returning the whole thing in one resources/list response becomes unwieldy, a documentation site with a thousand fixed pages, for instance. Staticness and size are independent concerns, a large but fixed set still benefits from pagination, covered in its own lesson later in this module, to avoid one giant response.

A large but static documentation set is still a very different problem from a genuinely dynamic one, since the pain here is purely about response size, not about the set changing underneath the client. Pagination solves the size problem cleanly while leaving the underlying staticness guarantee, same items, same order, fully intact across pages.
12. Static Resources at Server Startup

Many static resource servers compute their list once, at startup, by scanning a directory or reading a manifest file, and then hold that list in memory for the lifetime of the process. This is efficient and simple, but it does mean the server needs restarting, or an explicit refresh mechanism, if the underlying set of files genuinely changes, which is a reasonable tradeoff for something meant to represent a fixed set in the first place.
13. Static Resources and Version Control

Static resources map particularly well onto anything already tracked in version control, since a git repository is itself a fixed, enumerable tree at any given commit. A server exposing files from a specific commit or tag can build its static list directly from that tree, confident that it will not shift underneath it mid-session.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Pinning a static server to a specific commit or tag is a good way to guarantee reproducibility, since anyone who connects to that server sees exactly the same fixed tree regardless of when they connect.

blocks.text: 14. Static Resources in Practice: Config Files

Configuration is the textbook static resource use case, worth walking through concretely. An application ships with a known handful of config files baked into its deployment, and an MCP server built to help an assistant understand or troubleshoot that application can expose exactly those files as a fixed, named list, letting a client, or a model, browse and read them without needing any special discovery logic.

blocks.text: 15. Limitations of the Static Approach

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A static approach cannot represent content that changes at runtime

blocks.text: The static model breaks down the moment a domain genuinely needs items to appear or disappear based on something other than a server restart, live search results, rows a user is actively creating and deleting, currently connected devices. Forcing such a domain into a static shape, refreshing an in-memory list on a timer and hoping nobody notices the lag, tends to produce a resource set that quietly lies to the client about what currently exists.

Recognizing this boundary early saves a lot of awkward workarounds later. If the set of things you want to expose changes based on anything other than a deliberate server restart or explicit refresh, dynamic resources, the subject of the next lesson, are almost certainly the better fit.

items: A fixed list of currently online team members, which changes constantly and belongs to dynamic resources instead.
Search results over a document store, which depend entirely on the query a user just typed.
Rows returned from a live database query, which can change between one read and the next.

blocks.text: 16. Testing a Static Resource List

Because a static list is supposed to be identical across calls, it is one of the easiest things in an MCP server to write a solid automated test for: call resources/list twice, assert the two results are equal, and you have verified the core staticness guarantee. It is worth also asserting that every URI returned by the list actually resolves successfully through resources/read, catching any stale entries left behind after a refactor.
17. Static Resources and Multiple Clients

When several clients connect to the same static server at once, every one of them should see the exact same resource list, since staticness is a property of the server, not of any single connection. A server author should be wary of any implementation detail that accidentally scopes the resource list per client session, such as building it lazily from per-connection state, because that quietly breaks the guarantee that makes static resources useful in the first place.

This also means a static list is safe to share across an entire team using the same server deployment. Two engineers connecting to the same internal config server from two different editors should be browsing the identical set of config files, with no risk that one of them sees a slightly different view.
18. Refreshing a Static List When It Truly Must Change

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: The list truly needing to change points toward restarting the server

blocks.text: Even a static resource set occasionally needs to change, a new config file gets added during a deploy, an old style guide chapter gets retired. The right way to handle this is an explicit, visible event, a server restart, or a deliberate notification if the server and client both support list-change notifications, rather than silently mutating the in-memory list on a timer and hoping clients happen to re-fetch it.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: If changes to a static set are frequent enough that you find yourself building refresh logic for it, that is often a sign the resource is not truly static, and modeling it as dynamic from the start will save rework later.

blocks.text: Worked Example

Imagine building an MCP server for a small team's internal style guide, made up of exactly four fixed chapters: voice-and-tone.md, formatting.md, code-samples.md, and accessibility.md. None of these chapters get added or removed dynamically, new chapters only appear when someone on the team deliberately writes one and redeploys the server.

A client connecting to this server can safely cache this exact list for the whole session, present all four chapters in a picker immediately, and never worry about a fifth chapter silently appearing mid-conversation without an explicit reconnect.
Common Mistakes

items: Modeling a genuinely dynamic domain, like live search results, as a static list and refreshing it on a crude timer instead of embracing dynamic resources properly.
Recomputing the static list from scratch on every single resources/list call when it could be computed once and cached, wasting server work for no benefit.
Forgetting to keep the static list in sync after a deploy, leaving stale entries that no longer resolve through resources/read.
Returning entries in a random or unstable order across calls, which undermines a client's ability to treat the list as trustworthy and comparable.
Skipping description fields because the list is small, then wondering why a model has to fetch every resource just to figure out what each one is.

blocks.text: Practice

Design a static resource list for an MCP server that exposes a company's fixed set of onboarding documents: an offer letter template, an IT setup guide, a benefits overview, and a code of conduct. Write the JSON that resources/list would return, including a sensible URI scheme, name, and mimeType for each.
Key Takeaway

A static resource set is one whose membership is fixed and known at any given moment, the same list every time resources/list is called, even if the content behind individual entries can still change. That predictability is exactly what makes static resources cheap for a client to cache and easy to reason about, and it is the right model whenever a domain genuinely has a bounded, enumerable set of things to expose.

The next lesson turns to dynamic resources, where the set itself is generated or discovered on the fly, search results, live database rows, anything that cannot be written down ahead of time, and looks at how that changes both discovery and handling on the client side.
